title: 50 day trips every new Seattleite has to take
subtitle: Sorted by vibe, from 30 minutes out to make-it-a-weekend
author: Jeff Reynolds | Compass
drive_time_basis: Drive times are door to door from downtown Seattle on a clear Saturday morning. Ferry crossings are counted. Ferry lines and traffic are not.

vibes.tagline: Ferries, islands, harbor towns and the Sound
launch_points: Downtown and Belltown (walk-on ferries at Colman Dock)

vibes.label: Lake vibe
vibes.tagline: Glacier-blue water from the Olympics to the dry side
launch_points: Downtown (Bainbridge ferry for the Olympic lakes)

places.name: Bainbridge Island
places.why: Walk on the ferry at Colman Dock, and 35 minutes later you are strolling Winslow with the skyline behind you.
places.photo_alt: Waterfront homes and evergreens along the Bainbridge Island shoreline

places.name: Vashon Island
places.why: Farm stands, quiet beaches and Point Robinson Lighthouse, one short crossing from West Seattle.
places.photo_alt: A pod of orcas swimming past Vashon Island

places.name: Gig Harbor
places.why: A working harbor town with a fishing-fleet past. Walk Harborview Drive, then get on the water with Rainier in view on a clear day.
places.jeff_line: Where I grew up. Still my favorite harbor on the Sound.
places.photo_alt: Aerial view of boats in Gig Harbor at sunset with Mount Rainier behind

places.name: Poulsbo
places.why: Little Norway on Liberty Bay: Scandinavian storefronts, a waterfront park and a boardwalk along the marina.
places.photo_alt: Antique street clock in downtown Poulsbo

places.name: La Conner
places.why: A small waterfront town on the Swinomish Channel. Time it for the Skagit tulips in April.
places.photo_alt: La Conner waterfront reflected in the Swinomish Channel

places.name: Deception Pass
places.why: The 1935 bridge hangs about 180 feet above a churning tidal current. Walk the span, then take the beach trails below.
places.photo_alt: Green steel arch of Deception Pass Bridge above turquoise water

places.name: Port Townsend
places.area: Quimper Peninsula, via the Edmonds-Kingston ferry
places.why: A Victorian seaport at the tip of the peninsula. Spend the afternoon in the bunkers and on the beach at Fort Worden.
places.photo_alt: Victorian brick buildings on the Port Townsend waterfront

places.name: San Juan Islands
places.why: Ferry to Friday Harbor, then Lime Kiln Point for the lighthouse and, in summer, a shot at orcas from shore.
places.pass: Ferry fare; Discover Pass at Lime Kiln
places.note: Reserve your car spot on the ferry.
places.photo_alt: San Juan Islands under a pink sunset sky

places.name: Lake Wenatchee
places.why: A glacial lake at the foot of the Cascades with a sandy state-park beach, about 25 minutes past Leavenworth.
places.photo_alt: Calm water and evergreens at Lake Wenatchee

places.name: Baker Lake
places.why: A long, glacier-fed reservoir under Mount Baker, with lakeside trails through old-growth forest.
places.pass: NW Forest Pass at some trailheads
places.photo_alt: Mount Shuksan rising above Baker Lake

places.name: Lake Cushman
places.why: Turquoise water in the southeast Olympics, with the Staircase trails at the far end of the gravel road.
places.photo_alt: Aerial view of turquoise Lake Cushman and the Olympic Mountains

places.name: Lake Crescent
places.why: Glacially carved, famously clear and deep blue. Pair it with the short trail to Marymere Falls.
places.photo_alt: Clear water and a wooden dock on Lake Crescent

places.name: Soap Lake
places.why: A mineral-heavy lake people have soaked in for generations, minutes from Dry Falls.
places.photo_alt: Rocks in calm water at Soap Lake near sunset

places.name: Banks Lake
places.why: A long reservoir between basalt canyon walls, with Steamboat Rock rising straight out of the water.
places.photo_alt: Steamboat Rock and Banks Lake in warm evening light

places.name: Lake Chelan
places.why: A 50-mile glacial lake in dry, sunny country. Swim in town, then taste at the wineries on the hillsides.
places.photo_alt: Lakeshore Trail above Lake Chelan on a blue sky day

places.name: Snoqualmie Falls
places.why: A 268-foot waterfall 35 minutes from downtown. The overlook is steps from the parking lot.
places.pass: Paid parking in the upper lot
places.photo_alt: Snoqualmie Falls in fall

places.name: Rattlesnake Ledge
places.why: About 4 miles round trip to a rock ledge high above Rattlesnake Lake. The classic first Seattle hike.
places.photo_alt: Rattlesnake Ledge overlooking the valley below

places.name: Mount Rainier: Paradise
places.why: Wildflower meadows in summer, snowshoes in winter, and the mountain filling the whole sky. Start with the Skyline Trail.
places.season: Year-round, wildflowers late July to August
places.photo_alt: Edith Creek crossing a summer meadow below Mount Rainier at Paradise

places.name: Mount Rainier: Sunrise
places.why: The highest point you can drive to in the park, with the mountain close enough to feel.
places.photo_alt: Mount Rainier at sunrise from Sunrise Point

places.name: North Cascades: Diablo Lake
places.why: Glacial silt turns Diablo Lake an unreal turquoise. Stop at the vista point, then push on to Washington Pass if you have daylight.
places.season: Spring to fall; Highway 20 closes for winter
places.photo_alt: Turquoise Diablo Lake from the overlook in the North Cascades

places.name: Colchuck Lake
places.why: 8 miles round trip and about 2,300 feet up to glacier-blue water under Dragontail Peak. The realistic day-hike version of the Enchantments.
places.pass: NW Forest Pass or $5 day fee; free day-use permit at the trailhead
places.season: Summer to October; access road typically closed November to May
places.note: No dogs. The lot fills early.
places.photo_alt: Turquoise Colchuck Lake below granite peaks

places.name: Artist Point
places.area: End of the Mount Baker Highway
places.why: Mount Baker and Mount Shuksan both in view from the end of the road.
places.season: Midsummer to fall, road snowbound the rest of the year
places.photo_alt: Mount Baker seen from the trails at Artist Point

places.name: Hurricane Ridge
places.area: Olympic National Park, above Port Angeles
places.why: Drive from Port Angeles up to a ridge about a mile high, staring straight into the Olympics.
places.note: Call the park road line (360-565-3131) before you go.
places.photo_alt: Hikers on a trail at Hurricane Ridge facing the Olympic Mountains

places.name: Mount St. Helens
places.why: The 1980 blast zone still reads like a geology textbook, with Coldwater Lake and the lower viewpoints along SR 504.
places.note: Johnston Ridge Observatory is closed while SR 504 is rebuilt. Check access before you go.
places.photo_alt: Summer wildflowers in front of Mount St. Helens

places.name: Woodinville
places.why: Over 100 tasting rooms 30 minutes from downtown. Wine country with no overnight required.
places.photo_alt: Quiet country road through green fields near Woodinville

places.name: Yakima Valley
places.why: Washington's first wine region: wineries, hop fields and fruit stands stretched across the valley.
places.season: Best May to October, harvest in fall
places.photo_alt: Vineyard rows in the Yakima Valley

places.name: Prosser
places.why: A small town packed with tasting rooms. The easy base for Yakima Valley wine.
places.photo_alt: Elevated view of the Yakima Valley with Mount Adams in the distance

places.name: Red Mountain
places.why: A tiny, sunbaked growing region above the Yakima River, known for big, bold reds.
places.photo_alt: Autumn vineyard rows on Red Mountain

places.name: Maryhill and the Columbia Gorge
places.why: Wine on the cliffs above the Columbia, plus the Maryhill Museum of Art and a full-size Stonehenge replica built as a WWI memorial.
places.photo_alt: Maryhill Stonehenge Memorial above the Columbia River Gorge

places.name: Walla Walla
places.why: More than 100 wineries and a walkable downtown built for tasting-room hopping.
places.note: Book a driver or stay the night.
places.photo_alt: First snow on the Blue Mountains above Walla Walla

places.name: Snohomish
places.why: Antique shops along First Street and a riverfront trail, 40 minutes north.
places.photo_alt: Historic brick storefront in downtown Snohomish

places.name: Roslyn and Cle Elum
places.why: Two old coal-mining towns a few miles apart in the Cascade foothills. Walk Roslyn's historic main street, then wander Cle Elum and the river trails nearby.
places.photo_alt: Overlook above Cle Elum and the Cascade foothills

places.name: Bellingham and Chuckanut Drive
places.why: Fairhaven's brick historic district, then Chuckanut Drive's cliffside views over Samish Bay.
places.photo_alt: Autumn forest above Samish Bay along Chuckanut Drive

places.name: Ellensburg
places.why: College-town cowboy country on the dry side, with a brick downtown and the Yakima River Canyon drive nearby.
places.photo_alt: The Yakima River winding through the canyon near Ellensburg

places.name: Leavenworth
places.why: A Bavarian-style village tucked into the Cascades. Go midweek or in shoulder season to dodge the crowds.
places.photo_alt: Aerial view of Leavenworth at sunset in December

places.name: Winthrop
places.why: An Old West storefront town in the Methow Valley, reached over the North Cascades Highway.
places.note: Highway 20 closes in winter, which adds hours via US 2.
places.photo_alt: Old wooden farmhouse in winter mist in the Methow Valley

places.name: Omak
places.why: Okanogan ranch country. Time it for the Omak Stampede in August and it becomes a trip you will talk about for years.
places.photo_alt: The Okanogan Valley near Omak

places.name: Spokane
places.why: A real city on the dry side, with Spokane Falls thundering through Riverfront Park right downtown.
places.photo_alt: Spokane Falls and the river through downtown Spokane at sunrise

places.name: Westport
places.why: A surf beach, a working fishing harbor and Grays Harbor Lighthouse, the tallest in the state.
places.photo_alt: Surf and wide sand at Westport

places.name: Lake Quinault
places.why: A rainforest lake ringed by old-growth giants, with an easy loop trail through the moss.
places.photo_alt: Fall color reflected in Lake Quinault

places.name: Cape Disappointment
places.why: Two lighthouses where the Columbia River meets the Pacific, with the long sweep of the Long Beach Peninsula next door.
places.photo_alt: Waves breaking below Cape Disappointment Lighthouse

places.name: Hoh Rain Forest
places.why: 12 to 14 feet of rain a year builds moss so thick it hushes everything. The Hall of Mosses loop is under a mile.
places.photo_alt: Empty road through the mossy Hoh Rain Forest

places.name: Rialto Beach
places.why: Sea stacks, giant drift logs and a beach walk north to Hole-in-the-Wall at low tide.
places.photo_alt: Sea stacks and surf at Rialto Beach

places.name: Ruby Beach
places.why: Reddish sand, sea stacks and tide pools, a short walk down from Highway 101.
places.photo_alt: Sea stacks and tide pools at Ruby Beach

places.name: Cape Flattery
places.why: The northwesternmost point of the contiguous U.S. A short boardwalk trail ends at cliffs, sea caves and Tatoosh Island.
places.pass: $20 Makah Recreation Pass per vehicle, good for the calendar year
places.note: Respect tribal land and stay in visitor areas.
places.photo_alt: Sea stacks off Cape Flattery at sunset

places.name: Vantage: Frenchman Coulee and Ginkgo
places.why: Basalt columns at Frenchman Coulee and petrified wood at Ginkgo Petrified Forest, both above the Columbia.
places.photo_alt: Basalt columns at Frenchman Coulee near Vantage

places.name: Dry Falls
places.why: A 3.5-mile-wide, 400-foot cliff carved by Ice Age floods, once a waterfall that dwarfed Niagara.
places.photo_alt: The cliffs and lakes of Dry Falls

places.name: Grand Coulee Dam
places.why: One of the largest concrete structures in North America. Summer nights bring a laser light show on the spillway.
places.photo_alt: Grand Coulee Dam and town from Crown Point

places.name: Palouse Falls
places.why: A 198-foot drop into a basalt bowl, and Washington's official state waterfall.
places.note: Pair with Walla Walla for a weekend.
places.photo_alt: Palouse Falls dropping into a basalt canyon

places.name: Steptoe Butte
places.why: A summit road above the rolling Palouse wheat hills. Go at golden hour.
places.season: Greenest in May and June, gold in late summer
places.photo_alt: Rolling Palouse farmland at sunset from Steptoe Butte

web_subhead: Fifty places within a tank of gas, sorted by the kind of day you want, with drive times, passes and the best season for each one.

hero.alt: A parent carrying a child on a trail toward Mount Rainier

before_you_go.intro: Most of these trips need a pass, and several sit behind a road that closes for winter. Sort it out the night before.

passes.name: Discover Pass
passes.text: State parks and DNR land. $45 a year, or buy a day pass online or at the trailhead kiosk.

passes.name: Northwest Forest Pass
passes.text: Forest Service trailheads like Colchuck, Artist Point and some Baker Lake trailheads. $30 a year or $5 a day. The America the Beautiful pass covers it.

passes.name: National park entrance
passes.text: Mount Rainier and Olympic charge per vehicle. The America the Beautiful annual pass ($80 for US residents) covers both for a year.

passes.name: Sno-Park permit
passes.text: Required November through April at plowed winter lots.

passes.name: Makah Recreation Pass
passes.text: $20 per vehicle for Cape Flattery and Shi Shi Beach, good for the calendar year. Buy it in Neah Bay.

passes.name: Ferries
passes.text: Reserve a car spot for the San Juan Islands. Most other routes are first come, first served.

roads.name: Highway 20 over Washington Pass
roads.text: Closes roughly November through May. Diablo Lake stays reachable from the west side most winters, but the drive over to Winthrop does not.

roads.name: Chinook and Cayuse passes
roads.text: Highways 410 and 123 close November through late May.

roads.name: Mount Rainier: Sunrise road
roads.text: Open roughly early July to early October. Paradise stays open year-round with chains in the car.

roads.name: Artist Point
roads.text: The last stretch of Highway 542 opens midsummer and closes with the first big snow, usually in October.

roads.name: Hurricane Ridge
roads.text: Daily access in summer. Winter access is limited and weather dependent, so call the park road line (360-565-3131) before you go.

roads.name: Snoqualmie and Stevens passes
roads.text: Traction tires advised and chains sometimes required November through March. Check WSDOT before you leave.
